title: Zuckerberg Wants to Keep His Votes

illustration.alt: Mark Zuckerberg holds high-vote Meta Class B shares while zero-vote Class C shares flow toward a California tax envelope and an AI data center under construction.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Meta will distribute one zero-vote Class C share for every existing Class A or Class B share. Zuckerberg may immediately sell up to 20% of his Class C distribution without losing votes, while the remaining 80% is subject to a stapling condition; Meta can also issue nonvoting shares to raise capital without diluting his voting control.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Meta’s charter amendment required a shareholder vote, but Zuckerberg already controlled 61% of the votes and had approved it, so outside shareholders’ votes could not change the outcome—the vote about voting was effectively over already.

preschool.title: Meta’s Class C Shares That Never Say “Aye”
preschool.lesson: Meta plans to create nonvoting Class C shares so Mark Zuckerberg and the company can sell stock for taxes or AI investment without reducing his voting control, while limits on most of his new shares preserve some connection between ownership and control.
paragraphs:
Mark Zuckerberg owns about thirteen percent,
Yet sixty-one percent of Meta’s votes represent.
His Class B shares get ten votes apiece;
Class A gets one, so his control doesn’t cease.

But California’s Proposition 40 may bring
A multibillion-dollar tax bill in spring.
And Meta has $825 billion in AI commitments ahead—
For models and data centers, enormous sums may be spread.

Selling ordinary shares could shrink Mark’s command,
So Meta designed a new share for the plan:
Class C will have value, but voting gets none—
Not ten votes, not one vote, not even just one.

On January 19, 2027, shareholders are due
One new Class C share for each old share, too.
Mark should receive about 342 million that day;
The others, 3.4 billion, in the same giveaway.

Mark may sell twenty percent of his new stack,
Perhaps for a tax, while his votes stay intact.
The other eighty percent will be “stapled” instead:
To sell it, he must sell voting shares alongside the spread.

Meta can issue Class C to finance AI,
While Mark’s voting power stays sturdy and high.
The charter change technically needed a vote—
But Mark had sixty-one percent, so he’d already said “yes.”
Outside votes couldn’t alter the result in the least:
The vote about voting was over before it was released!

What happened? Meta proposed a 2-for-1-style distribution of zero-vote Class C shares, letting Zuckerberg sell some stock for a possible California wealth tax and letting Meta raise money for AI without immediately diluting his control. Because Zuckerberg already controlled about 61% of Meta’s votes, his approval made the required shareholder vote a done deal.

illustration.alt: Anthropic accountants watch convertible-note contracts grow heavier on a balance scale as the company’s valuation rises, pushing a net-loss ledger downward.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Convertible notes and other derivative-like financing instruments were remeasured at current value through the income statement, so Anthropic’s rising valuation created $72 billion of accounting charges.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Anthropic recorded an enormous loss largely because it became more valuable—an upside-down result summed up by “Could be worse!”}},

preschool.title: Anthropic’s Very Valuable Loss
preschool.lesson: When financing instruments are treated as derivatives, they are remeasured at current value; if the company’s value rises, the resulting accounting charge can reduce net income even without an equal cash payment.
paragraphs:
Anthropic planned an IPO, with shares for public sale,
But one line in its draft report made ordinary losses pale.

More than $80 billion lost in half a year!
Yet most was not a mountain of cash that disappeared.

Convertible notes had helped it gather funding first;
Their value climbed as Anthropic’s own valuation burst.

Accountants priced those promises again upon the books,
And $72 billion became charges—stranger than it looks.

The higher Anthropic’s value climbed, the bigger grew the cost;
By becoming more valuable, it booked a giant loss.

No ordinary business expense had caused that huge reverse:
A loss from growing valuable—well, it could be worse!

What happened? Anthropic reported a net loss of more than $80 billion for the first half of the year, including $72 billion in accounting charges from revaluing convertible notes and other financing instruments as the company’s value rose.

illustration.alt: University of Chicago protesters in Kalshi merchandise arrive by bus with breakfast outside CME Group to demand legal onion futures.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Commodity futures let farmers agree on a future sale price and hedge against price swings, but federal law has prohibited onion futures since 1958.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A quirky student crusade for the freedom to trade onion futures turned out to be sponsored—with a bus, breakfast, merchandise, and promotion—by Kalshi, a company whose business is creating betting markets on nearly everything.

preschool.title: The March for Onion Futures
preschool.lesson: Futures contracts let farmers lock in prices to reduce risk, but the Onion Futures Act of 1958 uniquely bans those contracts for onions; Kalshi sponsored a student protest seeking repeal.
paragraphs:
At the University of Chicago, a curious crowd
said, “Let onion futures be traded and allowed!”
About thirty marched by the Loop’s busy streets
to CME Group, where derivatives meet.

A futures contract sets tomorrow’s price today,
helping farmers hedge when crop prices sway.
Corn, wheat, and soy farmers may soften that risk,
but onions were crossed from the government’s list.

In the 1950s, some traders cornered the crop;
then the Onion Futures Act made onion contracts stop.
Since 1958, the ban has stayed strong—
though bets on weather and politics roll right along.

Adam Ash and For Our Futures joined the campaign.
The Chicago Maroon explained who helped with the train:
Kalshi paid for the bus, branded gear, and breakfast too,
then promoted the protest for more people to view.

Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour reposted the scene;
its video passed one million views on the screen.
Kalshi wants prediction markets on everything—
and onions are things. So the march had its spring.

The protest looked quirky, free-market, and bold:
students defending how onion crops might be sold.
Then came the punch line behind all the fun:
a betting-market company had sponsored the run.

What happened? Kalshi supported a protest by University of Chicago students and affiliates seeking repeal of the Onion Futures Act of 1958, which bans onion futures. Such contracts would let onion farmers lock in future prices and hedge against price changes, as farmers of crops such as corn, wheat, and soy can do.

illustration.alt: Jackie Reses looks delightedly surprised at a five-day calendar in a Goldman Sachs office, with her former Jersey Shore carnival stalls visible behind her.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: The Money Stuff writer moved from M&A law to corporate equity derivatives at Goldman Sachs for comparatively better hours; Jackie Reses later helped Square obtain banking capabilities and now runs Lead Bank, which supplies banking infrastructure to fintech companies.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Goldman Sachs, famous for punishing hours, felt like a lifestyle job to two people whose earlier work schedules were even more extreme—and Jackie Reses did not discover the five-day workweek until she joined it.

preschool.title: The Five-Day Surprise at Goldman Sachs
preschool.lesson: Jackie Reses helped Square, now Block Inc., become a bank and later ran Lead Bank, which provides banking infrastructure to financial-technology companies.
paragraphs:
At sixteen, Jackie Reses worked down by the shore,
Renting two boardwalk stalls—and then working some more.
Milk-can toss in one, flukey ball in the next;
The games helped pay for Wharton, where night classes cost less.

She helped her parents’ pharmaceutical businesses, too,
And thought working on Christmas was what people do.
Then Goldman Sachs brought an astonishing surprise:
A five-day workweek appeared before her eyes!

“I didn’t know that people worked five days a week
Until I went to Goldman Sachs,” Jackie would speak.
“I just assumed everyone worked on Christmas,” she said,
For that was the life her whole family had led.

The Money Stuff writer had once made a similar change:
From mergers-and-acquisitions law, with hours deranged,
To Goldman, arranging derivatives tied to company shares—
Still plenty of work, but with fewer late-night affairs.

He joked, “I’m the only one, surely it’s true,
Who went to Goldman for lifestyle!” Then Jackie made two.
Bloomberg’s Paige Smith found the better punch line:
At Goldman, five working days seemed simply divine.

Jackie helped Square—now Block Inc.—become a bank,
Then took Lead Bank’s top spot among its executive rank.
Lead powers fintech companies, helping services run:
Nubank, Stripe and Affirm are among them.

What happened? Jackie Reses grew up working extremely long weeks, so Goldman Sachs introduced her to the comparatively relaxed idea of working five days. She later helped Square become a bank and became CEO of Lead Bank, which supports major fintech companies.
